m6-t1.question: Which is the best problem statement for a capstone?
options: Small vegetable growers near Yelahanka need yesterday's prices at three nearby markets before choosing where to sell, because prices differ 20–40% and they rely on one trader's call
m6-t1.explanation: Specific user, job, pain and current workaround — and you can find five such users this week.

m6-t1.question: Which interview question yields the most reliable evidence?
options: Would you use an app that does X?
Tell me about the last time you did X — step by step, what did it cost you?
How much would you pay for X?
m6-t1.explanation: Past behaviour, time and money spent, and workarounds are evidence; hypotheticals produce polite yeses.

m6-t1.question: Who is usually your real competitor?
options: The user's current workaround — the phone call, the WhatsApp group, the notebook
m6-t1.explanation: You must explain why someone would switch from what they do today.

m6-t1.question: What does 'Wizard of Oz' mean in an MVP?
options: Doing steps manually behind the scenes so users experience the value before it is automated
m6-t1.explanation: You are testing whether users value the outcome, not whether you can automate it yet.

m6-t1.question: A good MVP statement includes:
options: Every feature you plan to build
One user type, one job, one channel and a numeric success measure by a date
m6-t1.explanation: The MVP exists to test the riskiest assumption with a number.

m6-t1.question: A founder says “students need an AI app” but has no specific user or task. What should the team do first?
options: Start with the most powerful model
Observe a specific user problem and write a narrow problem statement before choosing a solution
Estimate users from social media likes
m6-t1.explanation: Start with a real user problem, not an assumed technology solution.

m6-t1.question: An interview asks “Would you use our app?” Why is this weak evidence?
options: It invites polite speculation rather than describing observed past behaviour
m6-t1.explanation: Recent concrete behaviour is stronger than hypothetical intent.

m6-t1.question: A user currently solves a task with phone calls and a notebook. What might that reveal?
options: The user already has an AI app
The real competitor is the existing workaround
m6-t1.explanation: A product must improve on the current workaround.

m6-t1.question: A team’s market scan uses only AI-generated competitor names. What is missing?
options: Verification from real products, user interviews and current sources
m6-t1.explanation: Generated competitor lists need independent validation.

m6-t1.question: A problem statement lists five user groups and four jobs. What would make it testable?
options: Choose one user type, one job, one context and a measurable outcome
m6-t1.explanation: Narrow scope makes the hypothesis testable.

m6-t1.question: A team asks users what they disliked about a service. What follow-up gathers stronger evidence?
options: Ask whether they like the team
Suggest the answer and request agreement
Ask for the last specific occasion, the steps taken, the cost and what happened next
Ask only if they would pay
m6-t1.explanation: A detailed past episode reveals behaviour and pain.

m6-t1.question: A survey gets 80 responses from the team’s friends. What should the report say?
options: Expand the claim to all students
The sample is convenient and may not represent target users

m6-t1.question: A prototype tests a new registration workflow. What should success measure?
options: A user completing the target task with a defined time or error threshold
The quality of the mockup shadows
m6-t1.explanation: Measure user task completion, not design polish.

m6-t1.question: A founder wants to build all planned features before interviewing anyone. What is a better experiment?
options: Add features until the idea feels complete
Test the riskiest assumption with a small prototype or manual service first
Ask an AI to simulate customers
m6-t1.explanation: Early experiments reduce uncertainty before expensive builds.

m6-t1.question: Interviews reveal that the problem occurs once per year, not each week. What should the team reconsider?
options: Frequency, value and whether the solution should target another recurring task
The font of the problem statement
m6-t1.explanation: Problem frequency affects whether a recurring product provides enough value.

m6-t2.question: How many 'Must' stories should a one-week sprint have?
m6-t2.explanation: Three Musts with definitions of done keep the sprint focused and demo-able.

m6-t2.question: What is a 'definition of done'?
options: A concrete, checkable statement of what must be true for a story to be complete
m6-t2.explanation: If you cannot write the done statement, the story is not clear enough to build.

m6-t2.question: Before putting an AI prompt into an automation you should:
options: Test it in a chat with about twenty realistic inputs, including malformed ones, until it passes 19/20
Make it as long as possible
m6-t2.explanation: Prompts are tested in chat first; validation in the flow adds a second layer.

m6-t2.question: What should the daily build log contain?
options: Done items with names, decisions and reasons, blockers, evidence, tomorrow's plan and hours
m6-t2.explanation: The log is the team's proof of work and the source for the report and pitch.

m6-t2.question: What does 'always be demo-able' mean?
options: At the end of each day the product runs end to end, even with some manual steps
Only demo on the last day
m6-t2.explanation: Add features only in ways that keep the end-to-end flow working.

m6-t2.question: A one-week sprint backlog contains 14 must-have stories. What is the main risk?
options: The app will use fewer tokens
Too much scope prevents a reliable end-to-end demo
The team has too many test cases
m6-t2.explanation: A small sprint should focus on a few must-have outcomes.

m6-t2.question: A story says “AI works correctly.” Why is it not a good definition of done?
options: It is not observable or testable; define concrete behaviour and acceptance cases
m6-t2.explanation: A definition of done must describe checkable conditions.

m6-t2.question: A prompt works on five clean examples but fails on empty and malformed inputs. What should the team do?
options: Add realistic edge cases and fix the failure path before relying on the step

m6-t2.question: An AI feature uses user data but no owner field. What should the builder clarify?
options: The colour of the table header
Who can view, edit and maintain each record
m6-t2.explanation: Data ownership and permissions shape safe app behaviour.

m6-t2.question: A daily build log lists “worked on app” for every day. What would improve it?
options: Record completed tasks, decisions, blockers, evidence, next steps and time
m6-t2.explanation: A useful log shows what changed and why.

m6-t2.question: At the end of day two, the app requires a manual step but completes the user task. Is it demo-able?
options: No, every feature must be fully automated
Yes, if the team hides the manual step
Only if the model is proprietary
Yes, if the manual step is transparent and the flow works end to end
m6-t2.explanation: Always demo-able means a working end-to-end path, even when some steps are manual.

m6-t2.question: The team changes the data schema after building screens. What should it do?
options: Update screens, validation and tests together, then check existing records
Ask users to re-enter every record without notice
m6-t2.explanation: Schema changes require coordinated updates and migration checks.

m6-t2.question: A sprint AI prompt produces a useful answer but frequently includes extra prose around JSON. What can help?
options: Use a strict schema, parse validation and a safe retry or review path
m6-t2.explanation: Structured output needs constraints and validation.

m6-t2.question: A demo uses fabricated user statistics to look complete. What is the ethical alternative?
options: Present the values as a pilot result
Remove the labels but keep the numbers
Label sample data clearly and show actual evidence separately
Say the model generated the metrics
m6-t2.explanation: Demonstration data must not be represented as real user evidence.

m6-t2.question: A feature is almost finished but has no automated or manual test. What belongs in “done”?
options: A reproducible test showing its acceptance criteria pass
m6-t2.explanation: Completed work includes evidence that it meets the agreed criteria.

m6-t3.question: Which of these is an integration problem rather than an AI problem?
options: Phone numbers saved without a country code so messages fail
m6-t3.explanation: Formats, identity, timing, permissions and idempotence are the joins between tools.

m6-t3.question: What does 'idempotent' mean for your flow?
options: Running it twice by accident does not send the user two messages
m6-t3.explanation: A 'sent' flag checked before sending prevents duplicates.

m6-t3.question: How should the product behave when the AI step fails?
options: Degrade gracefully — send the template or a 'delayed' message — and queue the item for review
m6-t3.explanation: Detect, degrade, instruct the user, never silently drop, notify a human.

m6-t3.question: What must a pilot's privacy notice include?
options: Legal jargon copied from a large company
What is collected, why, who sees it, how long, how to leave or delete, and a contact — in plain language
m6-t3.explanation: Plain, specific, in the users' language, with STOP/DELETE that actually work.

m6-t3.question: How should you launch?
options: Team phones → three friendly users → pilot group, with honest framing and a decision date
Only after the product is perfect
m6-t3.explanation: Launch small, monitor, and keep the kill switch handy.

m6-t3.question: An automation sends the same confirmation twice after a retry. Which property would prevent this?
An AI service fails during a pilot. What should the user experience?
options: A clear delay or fallback with the task queued for human review
An empty screen that loses data
m6-t3.explanation: Graceful degradation preserves work and informs the user.

m6-t3.question: A privacy notice says “we value your privacy” but no specifics. What is missing?
options: Collected data, purpose, access, retention, deletion choices and a contact
A guarantee that no risk exists
m6-t3.explanation: A notice must explain actual data practices in understandable terms.

m6-t3.question: A pilot will use real students. What should be defined before recruitment?
options: The number of social posts only
Consent or notice, data minimisation, access, support route and stop conditions
A plan to keep every record forever
m6-t3.explanation: A pilot needs participant protections and operational boundaries.

m6-t3.question: An integration maps a phone number without country code, so messages fail. Is this an AI failure?
options: Yes; every integration problem is hallucination
Yes; the model must infer the country code
No; it is a data integration or validation problem
m6-t3.explanation: Many failures come from data contracts and integration, not model quality.

m6-t3.question: A launch checklist has a privacy review but no rollback plan. What is the gap?
options: There is no defined way to pause or revert if harm or failure appears
The app has too few users
The model needs a different name
m6-t3.explanation: Launch readiness includes a stop, rollback and incident process.

m6-t3.question: A new AI feature changes the output format used by an existing integration. What should the team do?
options: Test the contract end to end and deploy changes in a controlled sequence
m6-t3.explanation: Interfaces between systems must be validated after changes.

m6-t3.question: A pilot message may disclose a student’s fee balance to the wrong recipient. What control is essential?
options: Send to every contact in the file
Use AI to choose a likely recipient
Verify recipient identity and data access before sending, with human approval for uncertain cases
m6-t3.explanation: Recipient and permission checks prevent sensitive disclosures.

m6-t3.question: A team tests only on its own phones. What is missing?
options: Testing on representative devices, networks and user conditions
m6-t3.explanation: Real-world launch needs device and connectivity coverage.

m6-t3.question: A launch uses a short pilot with three friendly users. What is the honest framing?
options: A limited test whose findings may not generalise to all users
m6-t3.explanation: Pilot scope and evidence limits should be communicated accurately.

m6-t4.question: Which of these is a vanity metric?
options: Users who changed a market decision
Total sign-ups with almost no daily use
AI accuracy on the review sample
m6-t4.explanation: Lead with outcome and engagement; sign-ups alone say little.

m6-t4.question: How should AI be used to synthesise feedback?
options: Ask it to imagine what users probably think
Strictly from the feedback log: group into themes with counts and verbatims, adding nothing not in the data
m6-t4.explanation: AI groups and counts; you combine with numbers and decide.

m6-t4.question: When is 'stop' a successful capstone outcome?
options: When evidence shows no real pain after novelty fades, and the team documents what it learned
When the team runs out of time
m6-t4.explanation: The rubric rewards evidence and learning, not survival of the idea.

m6-t4.question: In the five-minute pitch, where does the technology belong?
options: After the hook, problem and user — around slide four, in one picture
m6-t4.explanation: Lead with the user and the number; show the architecture briefly; spend time on demo and evidence.

m6-t4.question: Why include a graceful failure in the demo?
options: It is the most credible evidence that the product is real and responsibly built
m6-t4.explanation: Showing failure handled builds trust; hiding it invites the hardest questions.

m6-t4.question: Sign-ups rise after launch, but few users complete the main task. Which metric is more diagnostic?
options: The percentage of target users who complete the task successfully
How many features are in the menu
m6-t4.explanation: Measure user outcomes tied to the problem.

m6-t4.question: AI summarises feedback and invents a quote not in the log. What should the team require?
options: Allow plausible quotes to improve the pitch
Use only logged responses, label counts and preserve verbatim evidence
Ask another model to approve the quote
m6-t4.explanation: Feedback synthesis must not fabricate evidence.

m6-t4.question: A pilot shows users do not have the assumed pain after novelty fades. What can be a successful decision?
options: Stop or pivot and document the evidence and learning
Claim high demand based on sign-ups
m6-t4.explanation: A reasoned stop prevents sunk-cost decisions and is a valid outcome.

m6-t4.question: A five-minute pitch spends three minutes describing model architecture before introducing the user. What should change?
options: Start with the team’s tool list
Lead with the user, problem and evidence; explain technology only as needed
m6-t4.explanation: The audience should understand the human problem before implementation detail.

m6-t4.question: A growth plan predicts ten thousand users without evidence. How should it be revised?
options: State assumptions, show a measured pilot baseline and propose a testable next step
Use a more precise invented number
Ask AI to approve the forecast
m6-t4.explanation: Forecasts should be transparent and grounded in evidence.

m6-t4.question: A user suggests a feature that conflicts with privacy safeguards. What should the team do?
options: Acknowledge the request, explain the trade-off and explore a safer way to meet the underlying need
m6-t4.explanation: Product decisions balance user value with safety and governance.

m6-t4.question: A pitch reports 90% satisfaction from 10 respondents. What context should accompany it?
options: A claim that the whole market agrees
Sample size, question wording, recruitment and limitations
m6-t4.explanation: Statistics need context to avoid overstating a small sample.

m6-t4.question: A team’s product is not ready for production but works as a prototype. How should it be presented?
options: Label it as a prototype and explain what is manual, tested and still unverified
m6-t4.explanation: Honest scope protects users and reviewers.

m6-t4.question: A demo fails once during rehearsal. What should the team prepare?
options: A truthful fallback or recorded walkthrough clearly labelled, while keeping the failure evidence
m6-t4.explanation: Responsible demos handle failure without misrepresenting results.

m6-t4.question: Which evidence best supports the claim that an app reduced processing time?
options: A defined before-and-after measurement with comparable cases and documented method
A screenshot of the home page
m6-t4.explanation: Performance claims need a reproducible comparison.

questions.question: A capstone team has a polished prototype but no evidence that users need it. What should the team do before adding features?
options: Build more screens to impress reviewers
Ask a language model to confirm market demand
Interview target users about a recent real instance of the problem and test the current workaround
Count team members who like the idea
questions.explanation: Recent behaviour and existing workarounds are stronger evidence than opinions or model-generated market claims.

questions.question: A team tests an AI intake prompt on 20 realistic cases and it passes 16. What is the safest launch decision?
options: Fix the failure modes and retest; keep a human checkpoint until the defined acceptance threshold is met
Hide the four failures from the demo
Increase temperature to make outputs more varied
questions.explanation: A missed threshold and known failures require remediation and human review before release.

questions.question: A message automation sends a duplicate reminder when a job retries. Which design control addresses the cause?
options: An idempotent operation keyed to the student and reminder period
questions.explanation: Idempotency makes retries safe and prevents duplicate external actions.

questions.question: A team’s pilot metric is “number of accounts created,” but most users never return. What is a better measure?
options: A behaviour linked to the user problem, such as successful task completion or repeat use after the novelty period
questions.explanation: Measure whether users achieve the intended outcome, not a vanity activity count.

questions.question: A product needs two weeks to validate the concept, but the college requests a permanent rollout immediately. What is the best proposal?
options: Agree to full rollout without measurement
Offer a limited pilot with a named owner, a numeric success threshold, risk controls and a decision date
Promise that AI will improve all outcomes
questions.explanation: A bounded pilot reduces commitment while defining evidence needed for a decision.

questions.question: A student-support MVP will store student questions and phone numbers. What must its plain-language notice cover?
options: What is collected, why, who can access it, retention/deletion, user choices and a contact
A promise that data is completely risk-free
questions.explanation: Users need an honest explanation of collection, purpose, access, retention and choices.

questions.question: The team’s AI provider is unavailable during a demo. What behaviour best proves production readiness?
options: Show a safe fallback, mark the item for human review and explain the failure path
Pretend the generated answer was real
Restart until it works and hide the delay
questions.explanation: Responsible products handle failure transparently rather than masking it.

questions.question: Feedback notes contain five complaints about the same delay. How should AI help synthesise them?
options: Add a likely sixth complaint to improve the summary
Convert every complaint to a positive quote
Discard raw feedback after the summary
Group only the recorded evidence, report counts and verbatim examples, and label uncertainty
questions.explanation: Synthesis must stay grounded in the feedback log and preserve traceable evidence.

questions.question: A team cannot recruit enough users to test every automated step. What is a useful early MVP method?
options: Claim the automated backend is complete
Use a Wizard-of-Oz process transparently in the pilot, manually performing steps while testing user value
Wait until every feature is built
questions.explanation: Manual work behind the scenes can test value before automation, provided evidence is not misrepresented.

questions.question: After a pilot, use is high during the first week and near zero later. What should the team conclude?
options: The product is proven because sign-ups were high
Investigate whether it solves a recurring problem; adjust or stop based on sustained evidence, not novelty
Exclude inactive users from the report
questions.explanation: Retention and repeated task success matter more than launch-day interest.
